title: Binary Search Variations
tagline: lower_bound, upper_bound, and 'search on the answer' — the patterns interviews actually test.

intuition.analogy: Plain binary search asks 'is X here?'. The variations ask sharper questions: 'where would X fit?', 'what's the first thing ≥ X?', 'what's the smallest value that makes this work?'. Same dictionary, smarter questions.
paragraphs: Most real binary-search problems are not 'find this exact element'. They're boundary problems: find the first index where a condition becomes true. If you can phrase your problem as a monotonic predicate — false, false, …, false, true, true, … — then binary search finds the flip point.

lower_bound finds the first element ≥ target; upper_bound finds the first element > target. Together they give you the count of a value, insertion positions, and range queries. The same skeleton, with the comparison flipped, solves all of them.

The most powerful variation is 'binary search on the answer'. When the answer itself is monotonic — e.g. 'if speed k finishes in time, so does k+1' — you binary search over the answer range and use a feasibility check as the predicate.
intuition.keyIdea: Binary search works on any monotonic predicate, not just on array values. Find the boundary where false flips to true.

steps.title: Frame a monotonic predicate
steps.detail: Define check(x) that is false for small x and true for large x (or vice-versa). The array values being sorted is just the simplest such predicate.

steps.title: Search the boundary, keep a half-open window
steps.detail: Use lo = 0, hi = n. When check(mid) is true, the answer is mid or earlier → hi = mid. Otherwise lo = mid + 1. The loop runs while lo < hi.

steps.title: lo converges to the boundary
steps.detail: When lo == hi, that's the first index where the predicate is true (or n if it never is).

complexity.timeReason: Same halving, but each step pays the cost of evaluating the predicate (often O(n) for 'search on the answer' problems).

pitfalls: Mixing the [lo, hi] (closed) and [lo, hi) (half-open) styles in one function — pick one and stay consistent.
Wrong predicate direction: make sure it really is monotonic (all-false then all-true).
Returning mid instead of lo — the converged lo is the boundary, not the last probed mid.

dryRun.clickMoment: lower_bound never short-circuits on equality. By always moving hi on '≥', it keeps sliding left to find the very first match — that's why it returns the leftmost 4, not just any 4.

problems.title: Search Insert Position
problems.statement: Return the index where target is, or where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

approach: This is exactly lower_bound: the first index where a[i] >= target. If the target is present it returns its position; otherwise the insertion point.
Use the half-open window [0, n]; collapse toward the first index whose value is >= target.

problems.title: First and Last Position
problems.statement: Find the starting and ending index of a target value in a sorted array.
problems.hint: lower_bound(target) gives the start; lower_bound(target+1) - 1 gives the end.

approach: Run two boundary searches. lower_bound finds the first index with value >= target; upper_bound finds the first index with value > target.
The range is [lower, upper-1]. If lower == upper the target is absent, so return [-1, -1].

problems.title: Capacity to Ship Packages
problems.statement: Find the least ship capacity to deliver all packages within D days.
problems.hint: Binary search on capacity; feasible(cap) = can we finish within D days?

approach: Binary search on the answer: the ship capacity. feasible(cap) = number of days needed when no day exceeds cap; it is monotonic (bigger capacity never needs more days).
The capacity must be at least max(weight) and at most sum(weights). Find the smallest capacity that ships within D days by a greedy day-count simulation.

problems.title: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.statement: Split the array into k subarrays minimising the largest subarray sum.
problems.hint: Binary search the largest-sum value; greedily count how many pieces it forces.
problems.tests: Answer-space search with a greedy predicate.

approach: Identical pattern to ship-packages: binary search the largest allowed subarray sum. feasible(cap) = minimum number of subarrays whose sums each stay <= cap.
Search cap in [max(nums), sum(nums)]; greedily start a new subarray whenever adding the next element would exceed cap. The smallest cap needing <= k subarrays is the answer.

problems.title: Find Peak Element
problems.statement: Find any peak (an element greater than its neighbours) in O(log n).
problems.hint: Compare mid with mid+1; move toward the higher side — a peak must exist there.
problems.tests: Binary search without a globally sorted array.

approach: A peak is any element greater than its neighbors; with nums[-1] = nums[n] = -infinity a peak always exists. Binary search on the slope.
If a[mid] < a[mid+1] an ascending slope guarantees a peak to the right (lo = mid+1); otherwise a peak is at mid or to the left (hi = mid).
